item.title: YunLone Galaxy star projector review — a sub-$30 customizable night light
item.description: null The YunLone Galaxy Projector is an inexpensive but effective way to bring the marvel of space into your living room or bedroom. Costing around $28, this star projector can display beautiful dancing auroras across your walls and ceiling, and thanks to app support, a huge range of color options are available. In fact, the color combinations you can display here are almost infinite. Key specs Size: 3.54 x 3.15 x 4.72 inches (9 x 8 x 12 cm) Weight: 17.6 ounces (500 g) Bulb Type: LED Laser: Yes Operation: App and remote control Rotation: Yes Sleep timer: Yes Speaker: Yes With built-in sounds, a Bluetooth speaker and endless customization options, this really is an all-singing, all-dancing star projector. We're amazed at just how much is loaded into this package for such a low price. It's surprisingly good quality, too, with the unit itself being sturdy and made out of hard-wearing plastic. This isn't a scientific star projector, of course. For that, we'd recommend the Sega Toys Homestar Classic or the Hommkiety Galaxy Projector . But even though the YunLone Galaxy Projector won't give you an accurate view of the Northern Hemisphere's night sky or a close-up of the moon, it's still a projector we recommend. If you're looking to create a relaxing atmosphere, it's one of the best star projectors we've reviewed. YunLone Galaxy Projector: Design The Yunlone Galaxy Projector has a simple but effective design. Kim Snaith The Yunlone Galaxy Projector has a simple but effective design. Kim Snaith Solid build quality Functional rather than aesthetic design Limited buttons on the front of the unit The YunLone Galaxy Projector doesn't have the most attractive design: It's clearly built for functionality rather than aesthetics. If an aesthetically pleasing projector unit is what you're looking for, perhaps consider the Jiawen Galaxy Projector Light . You won't find nearly as many functions as the YunLone Galaxy Projector packs in, however. That isn't to say that the YunLone Galaxy Projector is ugly, though. The design is basic, with a circular shape that houses a clear globe in the middle that acts as the projector. It sits on rubberized feet, so it doesn't easily slip or move around, and it's naturally tilted, so it points slightly diagonally rather than straight up. If you're buying for a child's bedroom, you don't need to worry about little hands being too rough when using it. item.title: Double asteroid solar eclipse caught on camera | Space photo of the day for Nov. 24, 2026
item.description: null (Image credit: ESA) A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another. What is it? The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system , which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system. Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Why is it incredible? For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet. Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

Held under the theme “Celebrating Partnerships, Rewarding Excellence,” the event brought together company leadership and long-standing partners from Northern, Eastern and Western Nigeria. It paid tribute to the distributors who built markets and the dealers who remained committed through shifting economic conditions. Their enterprise and confidence have carried CFM’s products to customers and communities across the country. The highlight of the evening was the rewarding of CFM’s best-performing dealers across three categories: Trailblazer, Sterling and Titan. Winners received 5-tonne, 10-tonne and 15-tonne trucks, as well as baking ovens. The night closed with the presentation of a 45-tonne truck to the overall best-performing dealer. L-R: Charles Babarimisa, Head of Sales; Siddharth Suri, Vice President/Business Head; Nitin Mehta, Managing Director, all of Crown Flour Mill (CFM) Limited; and Alhaji Oluwasesan Sose, the overall best-performing distributor and winner of a 45-tonne truck, during the presentation of award prizes. Nitin Mehta, Business Head, Wheat Milling & Pasta Business, Olam Agri, said the milestone reflects far more than time. “Fifteen years of growing together represents relationships built on trust, shared ambition and resilience. Bolaji Anifowose , Vice President & Commercial, Olam Agri, described dealers as strategic partners rather than an extension of the distribution network. “Their market knowledge, entrepreneurial drive and commitment connect our brands to consumers across the country. It has been a journey of learning, overcoming challenges and identifying opportunities together. This recognition encourages me to keep striving for excellence.” The runner-up, Opeyemi Sanusi Modinat, praised the company’s collaborative approach. “Our partnership has given us opportunities to grow, expand our market presence and serve more customers. What makes it special is the understanding that our success matters too.

item.title: China launches Pakistani astronaut to Tiangong space station, its 1st international visitor, alongside Shenzhou-24 crew (video)
item.description: null China launched an international astronaut, Pakistan's first space traveler to reach orbit, to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program. A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026. (Image credit: CCTV) Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong space station , a three-module orbital lab that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022. Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023 .) The Chinese Manned Space Engineering (Image credit: VCG/VCG via Getty Images) China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025 , with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training. We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch. This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest. The six astronauts of China's Shenzhou-23 and Shenzhou-24 crews give thumb's up signs in blue jumpsuits on the Tiangong Space Station. (Image credit: CMSE) Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu. Pakistan's first orbital astronaut, pilot Mohammed Zishan Ali (left), salutes alongside Shenzhou-24 crewmates Tang Hongbo (center) and Wu Yi before their launch into orbit. (Image credit: Xu Xun/VCG via Getty Images) Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24 . According to the South China Mor

item.title: Russia launches Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station (video)
item.description: null Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station. The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. If all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long. A Russian Soyuz rocket launches the uncrewed Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station from Baikonur Cosmodrome, Kazakhstan on Nov. 24, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The cosmonauts currently living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module. The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019. Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com. Progress 96 cargo spacecraft packed with science and supplies approaches the International Space Station for a docking on Sept. 19, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays. Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere . Japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only currently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

item.description: null Editor's Note: The November full supermoon dazzled stargazers with a spectacular show overnight on Nov. 24. Check out our photo wrap article to see spectacular images of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world. November's full moon rises tonight (Nov. 24)! You can see live telescopic views of the "Beaver supermoon" courtesy of the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP). The free YouTube livestream begins at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) and will feature live views of the moon captured by a suite of robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting. Today's stream features expert commentary from VTP founder Gianluca Masi, along with photos of previous full moons shining above historic landmarks in the heart of Rome. What makes the November full moon special? November's full moon is often called the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the industrious animals are hard at work building dams and preparing for the winter months, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . It is also set to be a spectacular supermoon , which reaches peak illumination while within 90% of perigee — the closest point to Earth in the moon's 27-day elliptical orbit. You might like: November full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Beaver Moon . Supermoons can be up to 13% larger and 30% brighter than the smallest full moon of the year, which occurred in May earlier this year as the natural satellite shone opposite the sun in Earth's sky while close to apogee, when it is farthest from our planet. item.title: Nigeria and Tanzania to Co-Host Inaugural WHAS in Abuja, Mobilising Continental Action for Better Women’s Health
item.description: The Governments of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the United Republic of Tanzania will jointly host the inaugural Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) 2026 on Tuesday, 1 December 2026, at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja, from 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM. Held under the theme “Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health,” WHAS 2026 will convene approximately 300 senior decision-makers, including Heads of State, First Ladies, Ministers of Health and Finance, African Union (AU) leadership, development finance institutions, philanthropists, and health innovators, to move Africa from political commitment to accountable investment and delivery. As a Nigeria-led, African-owned continental platform, WHAS is designed to advance women’s health across the entire life course, encompassing maternal, reproductive, and gynaecological health, noncommunicable diseases, and menopause, by treating women’s health not merely as a social priority, but as a central driver of Africa’s economic and social progress. Investing in women’s health is also an investment in Africa’s productivity, economic resilience, and future prosperity. WHAS 2026 bridges the flagship African Union Champion mandates of the two co-hosting nations. Serving as founding convener, Nigeria brings the political leadership and health workforce agenda championed by His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, AU Champion for Human Resources for Health and Community Health Delivery Partnership. Nationally, WHAS is anchored in the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare under the leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, CON , with presidential facilitation by the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Women’s Health (OSSAP-WH) . As co-host, Tanzania brings its continental leadership on maternal and child health, championed by Her Excellency, President Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, AU Champion for Maternal and Child Health, advancing the Continental Roadmap on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) 2026–2030 and its Three Zeros: Zero Home Delivery, Zero Preventable Maternal and Newborn Deaths, and Zero Unvaccinated Children. Tanzania’s co-hosting is delivered through the Ministry of Health, led by Hon. Mohamed Omary Mchengerwa , Minister of Health, and the Secretariat of the African Union Champion for Maternal and Child Health. Speaking ahead of WHAS 2026, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, CON , Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, described the Summit as an important platform for advancing collaboration, shared learning, and African ownership of the women’s health agenda: “ The Women’s Health Africa Summit is a great platform for bringing together leaders, advocates, practitioners, academics and financiers to identify gaps, mobilise action and facilitate shared learning across countries. item.title: How Williams Alamu Graduated with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan
item.description: Williams Alamu marks his B.Sc. First-Class Honours graduation in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. There was a time when Williams Alamu would rather not sit an examination than risk getting a grade he wasn’t happy with. A B or a C in his Cambridge A-levels felt like a possibility he wasn’t ready to entertain, so he didn’t write the exams. A few years later, at 23, he has graduated from the University of Ibadan with a B.Sc. in Statistics, First-Class Honours and a CGPA of 3.65/4.0. Somewhere along the way, he decided that fear was no longer going to make his decisions for him. When Williams got into UI, he had a rather ambitious plan: become the Best Graduating Student in his faculty. Getting there would require more than good intentions. There were 5:30am wake-ups, difficult Statistics courses, friends who became unofficial tutors, a ChatGPT Pro subscription in 300 level, job offers he turned down and one Demography exam that kept him awake for 36 hours. University, as it turns out, came with quite a few plot twists. In this interview with BellaNaija, Williams takes us through the habits, people and decisions that shaped his academic journey. He also tells us whether he got that coveted top spot, what he learnt from the opportunities he put on hold, and what he would tell another student hoping to graduate with First-Class Honours. If that’s a goal you’re working towards, you may want to take notes. Literally or otherwise. Williams Alamu celebrates graduating with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. At what point did you realise you were chasing a record-breaking grade? Was it a goal from Day 1, or did it evolve? It was a goal from day one, actually. When I gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I already had my mind set on graduating as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty. I knew becoming the overall Best Graduating Student in the university would require an extraordinary amount of work, but I felt being the best in my faculty was something I wanted to work towards. And, of course, that would also mean graduating as the best student in my department. The motivation behind that goal goes back to shortly after secondary school, when my parents enrolled me in a Cambridge A-level programme. I went into it hoping to achieve three A-stars, but Chemistry was a major struggle. As the examinations approached, I became increasingly worried about my performance. I think I was more afraid of not meeting my own expectations than I was of the examination itself. The thought of getting a B or C frightened me so much that I eventually decided not to sit for the examinations. Williams Alamu seated in a University of Ibadan lecture hall before a test during his Statistics degree. When I eventually gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I didn’t want to repeat that experience. I saw university as an opportunity to approach things differently. item.title: My Experience at the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos
item.description: The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. When I got the email that I was selected for the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos, I knew, without doubt, that the cohort of writers I would engage with would be some of the finest around. I was not disappointed. The workshop put me in the same room with extremely talented writers I had read and admired from a distance. Some of us have shared publication credits and honours on longlists and shortlists of literary prizes over the past couple of years. For two days, we were guests of the British Council and students at the feet of our primary facilitator, Nigerian writer, journalist, and editor, Molara Wood . Liberian-American writer Wayétu Moore also facilitated a session, and a publishing masterclass was held by Anwuli Ojogwu and Eghosa Imasuen of Narrative Landscape Press. The twelve selected writers for the workshop are Azeeza Adeowu, Chinenye Okechukwu, Ahmad Adedimeji Amobi, Chinonso Nzeh, Innocent Chizaram Ilo, Kingsley Alumona, Mayowa Fagbure, Mustapha Enesi, Oluwatobi Afolabi, Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé, Ufuoma Bakporhe, and Winifred Odunoku. A combination of writers who are also journalists, editors, filmmakers, among other things. “Gotta Whack That Guy!” I first encountered Molara Wood on social media, where she shared her commentary on a plethora of issues, from literature and culture to politics. So I particularly looked forward to learning from her. On the first day, when I walked into the workshop at the British Council, she was there, standing and already conversing with the writers present. By the time other writers arrived and the round of introductions began, it illuminated the sort of people I was in the room with. I had read the writing samples and excerpts recommended for reading ahead of the workshop. They were really good. These writers seemed assured in their craft, and it became further obvious as the conversations became robust. Molara Wood, with all her brilliance, struck me even more with the animated manner in which she facilitated the workshop. As though she was more excited to teach than we were to be taught by her. This made the workshop flow seamlessly from the jump. We shared opinions on the assigned short stories. We discussed how well they used dialogue, descriptions, and language to reveal so much about the characters and the world they inhabit. We discussed how words, accents, and other idiosyncrasies of characters can reveal class, age and societal standing. This is why it is important for writers to observe the world. To observe the minute details of what makes up people, because these are the tools through which subtext can be created. The arts are connected, especially through the basic principles of storytelling. Molara Wood recognised this by using the context of films, mostly classics, to highlight storytelling techniques for better understanding. item.title: November's full moon rises tonight! Here's how to see the Beaver Moon supermoon
item.description: null Editor's Note: The November full supermoon dazzled stargazers with a spectacular show overnight on Nov. 24. Check out our photo wrap article to see spectacular images of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world. Get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know. November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter. Viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The stream will feature live views of the lunar disk captured from the VTP's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting. The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon , because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee , when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon". When to see the Beaver Moon November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon. A supermoon can make for a spectacular sight when caught close to the horizon. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. If you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location. What should I expect from the November supermoon? You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering. Celestron Nexstar 4SE (Image credit: Celestron) This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. item.title: Temi Nkem’s Oversized Braided Updo Is the Hairstyle Inspiration We Needed
item.description: Big Brother Naija 2026 winner Temi Nkem pairs a structured matte-gold leather corset and black velvet skirt with an architectural braided updo. If your next braid appointment has you thinking beyond the usual ponytail or bun, Temi Nkem has an idea you might want to take to your hairstylist. The Big Brother Naija 2026 winner wore her thick braids in a high, sculptural updo, with oversized loops arranged into a crown. She paired it with a gold-and-black look, complete with metallic beauty details and contrasting textures. Rather than letting her thick braids fall down her back, Temi has gathered them into a sleek, high updo, building them into an oversized crown of interlocking loops. The result is sculptural, full of volume and beautifully structured. It’s also a great example of how to style thick braids when you want a fresh way to wear them for an event. Pulling the hair up keeps the face open, while the loops create plenty of interest around the crown. And with the base kept sleek, the hairstyle gets to take centre stage without feeling too busy. Temi Nkem accents her sleek looped braid updo with metallic gold-leaf detailing, brow crystal, and glossy nude lips. Then there are the beauty details. Temi goes for smoky brown eyeshadow, full lashes and a glossy nude lip outlined in brown, keeping the makeup warm and complementary to the outfit. A little gold takes things further: there’s a tiny cross-shaped crystal between her brows, three vertical micro-beads on her chin, hammered circular gold earrings and flecks of metallic gold leaf tracing the side of her face, from her left temple down to her collarbone. It’s an unexpected beauty detail, and one that ties in beautifully with the colours of her outfit. Temi Nkem shows how to style thick braids into a sculptural crown paired with a gold-and-black corset gown. Now, about that gown! Temi shows how to wear gold and black with ease, starting with a structured matte-gold leather corset bodice. It features vertical seam boning, a deep V-plunge neckline and a sharply defined V-shaped basque waist. Below it, a fitted black velvet skirt brings a different texture into the look, while matching off-the-shoulder velvet arm bands complete the silhouette. The contrast between the gold leather and plush black velvet is what makes the combination work so well. Rather than having both colours compete for attention, the matte gold adds warmth and the black velvet gives the outfit balance. So, if thick braids are next on your salon mood board, you might want to save Temi’s updo. And if you’re planning a gold-and-black outfit, her mix of leather and velvet is another styling idea worth keeping. item.title: Enoch Adeagbo Was Denied Admission for Being Too Young. At 19, He’s Set to Graduate with First-Class Honours
item.description: My name is Enoch Adeagbo. In 2021, at the age of 14, I was refused admission because I was too young. I was very sad because the reason had nothing to do with my academic ability. My parents encouraged me to apply to another university, and I eventually gained admission to Ajayi Crowther University (ACU), Oyo, at the age of 14. On Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at 19, I will graduate from ACU with First Class Honours in Civil Engineering, having earned a CGPA of 4.79 out of 5.00, as the second-best student in my department and the third-best student in the Faculty of Engineering. If I had given up and not applied to another school, I might not be here today sharing my journey. Where it all began As a child, I often accompanied my father to construction sites. I enjoyed watching structures take shape from foundation stage to completion. My interest in how buildings were designed and constructed gradually developed into a desire to become an engineer. At 14, however, I was considerably younger than most of my course mates. People frequently reminded me of my age, and I had to adjust. I learnt to focus on my studies, take part in university activities and make the most of the opportunity I had been given. In the 2022/2023 session, at 15, I received the Overall Best Student in Engineering of the Year award at the 200-level. I had not expected it, but it was also an encouraging recognition of my work, and it motivated me to stay consistent. The C that taught me something But being interested in a course does not necessarily mean you’d understand it completely. I learnt this in the first semester of 400 level, when I got a C in Structural Analysis, a three-unit course I thought I understood. I was surprised because I had been confident in my knowledge of the course. That experience made me reflect on my approach to studying. I became more deliberate about understanding concepts rather than simply assuming I had mastered them. Studying with a group and teaching my coursemates also became valuable. Explaining a topic to someone else also helped me understand the course more. More than lectures Beyond the classroom, I served as the Academic Officer of the Nigerian Universities Engineering Students’ Association (NUESA), ACU Chapter, for the 2025/2026 session. I also served as an Assistant Class Representative and was involved in chapel activities as a chapel worker. My faith in God has played an important role throughout my university journey. It shaped my discipline, decisions and priorities, and helped me remain intentional about my responsibilities. I am grateful to my parents, who made sure I did not have to worry about finances while pursuing my education. Their support allowed me to concentrate on my studies and other responsibilities without the additional burden of financial concerns. item.title: Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) Joins the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts in the UK
item.description: Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) joins the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts following his Master’s degree graduation in London. Photo Credit: Debo Adedayo/Instagram Have you been keeping up with Debo Adedayo lately? Because the Nigerian actor, content creator and activist—popularly known as Mr Macaroni —just added another major feather to his cap. Debo has officially joined the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts (RSA), a UK-based institution recognised globally for bringing together changemakers across the arts, social innovation and public life. Sharing the news with his followers, Debo kept his message warm and forward-looking: I am elated to join the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts. Looking forward to learning, sharing and collaborating with artists from around the world who are passionate about impacting our society for good. This recognition arrives right on the heels of a busy, rewarding season for the entertainer in London. Earlier this month, Debo graduated with a Master of Arts with Distinction in Performance (Acting) from the Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts, validated by the University of East Anglia, in the United Kingdom. During his postgraduate training at Mountview, he also made his UK stage debut in July, starring as Lord Commander Thomas Fairfax in Howard Brenton’s historical play 55 Days at The Backstage Theatre in Peckham, London. Debo Adedayo brings historical figure Lord Commander Thomas Fairfax to life in James Yeatman’s stage direction of 55 Days at Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts. Photo Credit: Debo Adedayo/Instagram Long before stepping onto the London theatre stage, Debo Adedayo (born Adebowale Babatunde Adedayo ) earned his first degree in Theatre Arts and Film Studies from Redeemer’s University in 2018. Millions first came to love him in 2019 through his satirical comedy skits—creating memorable characters like Daddy Wa and Professor Hard Life—while he has steadily built an acclaimed Nollywood film career alongside his civic advocacy in Nigeria. Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) holds his Master of Arts with Distinction certificate awarded by the University of East Anglia through Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts. item.title: The Design Table 2026 by So.Me Solutions: African Fashion in the Spotlight with $7,000 in Award Support for Emerging Designers
item.description: The Design Table 2026 brought together some of the voices, ideas and creative forces shaping African fashion for an afternoon of industry exchange, recognition and conversation. The annual cultural platform, produced by So.Me Solutions, welcomed designers, fashion entrepreneurs, industry leaders, media personalities and fashion enthusiasts for its latest edition. Held at GRAS Lagos, Victoria Island, during Lagos Fashion Week, this year’s gathering explored the people, perspectives and opportunities influencing the future of African fashion. The event also marked a significant milestone for So.Me Solutions, which celebrates 10 years as a 360 communications agency. Among the guests were Folake Amber (Tiffany Amber), Bola Balogun (Glam Brand), Sharon Adeleke, Beverly Naya, Awed by Moni, Marvy Olugu (House of Marvee) and Funmi Ford , alongside other familiar faces from across fashion, entertainment and the creative scene. A Seat at the Table for the Next Generation A major highlight of this year’s edition was the Next Gen Design Impact Award, which received 101 applications from emerging designers. Following the selection process, three finalists, Sultana, Dimeji Ilori and Bjuv Woman , were shortlisted for the award. The finalists were evaluated by a five-member jury comprising Dr. Yetty Ogunnubi, Odio Mimonet, Eniafe Momodu, Ugonna-Ora Owoh and Yoanna “Pepper”, with guests also participating in the voting process. Bhuv Woman emerged as the winner, receiving the $5,000 grand prize funded by Vlisco, Patrón and Culture Lab. In addition, Odio Mimonet extended a further $2,000 in award support, bringing the total prize support associated with the award to $7,000. Beyond the financial support, the winning package includes mentorship, industry access and opportunities to further advance the designer’s work. The announcement was an emotional moment for Bhuv Woman, who was visibly moved as she received the recognition and expressed gratitude to the organisers. Through the award, The Design Table continues to create opportunities for emerging designers to gain visibility, access and recognition while connecting them with established voices and resources within the fashion industry. Who Gets to Shape the Future of African Fashion? The conversations continued with a speakers session titled “ Who Gets to Shape the Future of African Fashion?” , moderated by Yvan Otu and featured Mai Atafo , founder of ATAFO; Ezinne Chinkata , founder of Zinkata; Sacha Okoh, fashion entrepreneur and creative director of Viva; Kiki Osinbajo , founder of CIAR; and Tess Tanaka, founder of Moda54. The session explored how African fashion can move beyond being treated as a niche category and become more firmly integrated into the wider global fashion landscape. Discussions touched on what it takes for African brands to be stocked, worn and embraced as part of everyday fashion, alongside the realities of production, pricing, distribution, customer experience and access to markets. item.title: Danielle Adewusi Honours Benin Kingdom Royalty in a Self-Designed National Costume at Miss Universe 2026
item.description: Danielle Adewusi displays the sweeping circular halo backpiece and floor-length beaded train of her Benin-inspired national costume. A little Benin royalty on the Miss Universe stage? Danielle Adewusi is bringing it to Puerto Rico. For the 75th edition of the competition in San Juan, Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 has arrived at the National Costume runway with Daughter of the Coral Throne, an Edo-inspired creation that brings the history of the ancient Benin Kingdom into the spotlight. And in case you missed that detail, Danielle designed the entire look herself. Now, where do we begin with this costume? The red coral beads are everywhere, from the sheer-panelled corset bodysuit and its sweetheart neckline, trimmed with gold-toned cowrie shells, to the floor-sweeping beaded overskirt and train. Look a little closer and there’s a miniature Queen Idia mask emblem at the hip. Danielle Adewusi holds her gold ceremonial staff diagonally across Daughter of the Coral Throne against a waterside garden backdrop. Then comes the fan-shaped coral bead headpiece, followed by a sweeping circular halo backpiece with cascading bead fringes. A tall gold ceremonial staff, topped with a sculpted Queen Idia mask, completes the look. Sculpted bronze-gold motifs and thousands of beads bring the whole tribute together, with each detail drawing from the artistry and royal traditions of the Benin Kingdom. Danielle Adewusi pairs warm bronzed makeup and sleek cornrows with red coral beadwork and gold cowrie detailing. Of course, Danielle isn’t leaving us to admire the costume without knowing what inspired it. She shared the story behind Daughter of the Coral Throne, explaining how she wanted to honour her Edo heritage and celebrate a kingdom whose history and identity remain, even after many of its treasures were taken: For my Miss Universe National Costume, I honour my Edo heritage and the extraordinary legacy of the ancient Kingdom of Benin, one of Africa’s greatest civilisations… Daughter of the Coral Throne reimagines the splendour of Edo royalty through contemporary African couture. Thousands of coral-inspired beads celebrate the prestige and authority of Benin royalty, while gold detailing pays tribute to the kingdom’s master craftsmen. The circular backpiece symbolises the continuity of our ancestry, radiating across generations. In my hand, a golden ceremonial staff honours the Oba of Benin, representing leadership, royal authority and an unbroken lineage. And as I follow in my mother’s footsteps, 35 years after she wore the Miss Universe Nigeria crown, I am reminded that legacy is not simply inherited. It is preserved, honoured and carried forward. Danielle Adewusi honours her Edo heritage in Daughter of the Coral Throne ahead of the Miss Universe 2026 finale There’s a personal connection to this Miss Universe journey, too. item.title: Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
item.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon. To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement . "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon." To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith , the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions. The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil. Oregon State University researchers David Handy and Aymeric Goyer studying potatoes grown in lunar regolith. (Image credit: Aymeric Goyer/David Handy/OSU) "We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement. The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth. NASA funding supported this research.

item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

item.title: Baby News and Beautiful Blue! Mitchel Ukachukwu Is Expecting Her First Child
item.description: Mitchel Ukachukwu celebrates her pregnancy announcement in a strapless pleated royal blue gown and neck scarf. Baby news and a beautiful maternity reveal? Congratulations are certainly in order for Mitchel Ukachukwu (née Ihezue )! The former Most Beautiful Girl in Nigeria (MBGN) and Miss Universe Nigeria titleholder is expecting her first child, and she’s sharing the lovely news with photographs that have us smiling and admiring her royal blue maternity look. If this is how Mitchel is introducing us to her maternity style, we’re already looking forward to more. For her pregnancy announcement, Mitchel slipped into a strapless, floor-length royal blue gown crafted from finely pleated, semi-sheer organza. The sweetheart neckline is gathered into a knot just above her baby bump, while the skirt falls into soft pleats, opening into a high front slit. She added a matching pleated neck scarf that flows into a long cape, with sweeping lengths of royal blue fabric suspended around her to complete the setting. Mitchel Ukachukwu marks her pregnancy reveal in a pleated royal blue gown with sweeping fabric waves. We also love how the beauty details bring everything together: chestnut-brown hair in glossy, side-parted Hollywood waves, soft bronzed makeup and understated gold jewellery. And, of course, those sweet photographs of her cradling her bump make the announcement all the more lovely. Many of us first got to know Mitchel as Mitchel Ihezue when she won the Most Beautiful Girl in Nigeria crown in 2017, before going on to claim the Miss Universe Nigeria title in 2023. Her pregnancy announcement comes nearly three years after she married Nigerian billionaire businessman and Prince Nicholas Ukachukwu , popularly known as Ikukuoma. The couple celebrated their union in December 2023 with traditional and white wedding ceremonies in Anambra State and are now preparing to welcome their first child. Mitchel Ukachukwu cradles her baby bump while wearing a knotted sweetheart royal blue gown and gold accessories. Sharing the news, Mitchel wrote, “Soooo….we cooked! The bestowment of God’s goodness. God is Faithful.” And they really did cook! With their first child on the way, Mitchel and Nicholas are getting ready for a new chapter together. We can’t be the only ones already looking forward to seeing how Mitchel styles her baby bump, can we? Mitchel Ukachukwu showcases the sheer pleated skirt and flowing cape of her royal blue maternity outfit. *** Photo Credit: Mitchel Ukachukwu/Instagram The post Baby News and Beautiful Blue! item.title: How to Style Green Lace for Asoebi Like Mercy Aigbe
item.description: Structural tailoring meets monochrome colour play in Mercy Aigbe’s olive and sage green asoebi look. Whenever a green dress code lands in your inbox for an upcoming wedding or celebration, the goal is always making the colour feel fresh and flattering rather than predictable. Nollywood star and filmmaker, Mercy Aigbe just gave us the sweetest blueprint for how to wear green lace for asoebi without letting heavy fabric wear you . The secret to nailing monochrome green for asoebi is mixing your shades and textures so you avoid one flat block of colour from head to toe. Mercy’s gown pairs a smooth, velvety olive corset—complete with visible boning and a central trail of beaded leaf appliqués—with a heavily beaded mermaid skirt in the same olive family . Mercy Aigbe showcases the full silhouette of her olive green corset and beaded lace mermaid gown paired with a marbled sage headtie. Keeping the bodice matte while the skirt sparkles lets the silhouette breathe, and crowning the outfit with a lighter, marbled sage headtie (gele) brightens up the face far better than a dark green wrap ever could. When taking your own green lace to the tailor, borrow her structural tricks: an asymmetrical off-the-shoulder neckline with 3D floral cutouts draws the eye upward, while a diagonal beaded sash-peplum along one hip creates curves without adding bulk around your waist. Mercy Aigbe pairs her olive green lace outfit with a deep red crystal crescent clutch and matching red manicure. As for how to accessorise a green monochrome outfit, skip the usual all-gold default and bring in a rich contrast colour. Olive and sage sit right opposite red on the colour wheel, which is why Mercy’s gold jewellery set with dark red stones, crescent red crystal clutch, and glossy red nails pop so well against the green . Paired with warm golden-bronze eyeshadow and a glossy nude-brown lip , the whole look feels balanced, celebratory, and ready for any guest list. Mercy Aigbe pairs her olive green lace outfit with a deep red crystal crescent clutch and matching red manicure. *** Photo Credit: Mercy Aigbe Adeoti/Instagram The post How to Style Green Lace for Asoebi Like Mercy Aigbe appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Temi Nkem, Big Brother Naija 11 Winner, Signs on as Checkers Custard Brand Ambassador
item.description: Official Unveiling of Temi Nkem and Karan Checker Temi Nkem (born Temitope Chigbue ), ultimate finalist of Big Brother Naija Show Ya Sef , the eleventh edition of Africa’s TV game show, added another feather to her cap just weeks after coming out tops at the eleventh edition of the DStv reality show. Checkers Custard , Nigeria’s custard brand, welcomed the starlet as chief brand influencer cum Brand Ambassador at a signing ceremony chaired by Karan Checker , Managing Director, Checkers Africa , at a ceremony witnessed by the media, friends, staff, influencers and a host of well-wishers. It’s a Homecoming! Karan Checker, Temi Nkem and Ashish Checker The entire continent of Africa witnessed the 21-year-old influencer’s genuine love for Checkers Custard during her ten-week stay in Big Brother’s house with the incessant trips to the kitchen primarily to make her favourite snack, in-between meal filler and as a whole meal with select pairings. Checkers Custard was central to her nutritional routine. File signing Temi came home. Temi Nkem x Checkers Custard Temi, at the winning prize presentation a few days after the grand finale, remarked, “ …we use Checkers Custard for our cake and custard in London. When I was telling everybody cake and custard is dessert, they were saying no, it’s breakfast, so I tried it the first time… it was ‘bussing’… I don’t know how to cook… but that one I needed to make sure I made sure I knew how to do, and I am so happy, so grateful” The British-born Nigerian Accounting & Finance undergrad came into the country solely to participate in the fiercely contested game show and excelled week in, week out, showing her prowess in executing a strategy of being herself, showing her resilience and goodly disposition. These traits did not go unnoticed as Checkers Custard’s brand handlers watched keenly, finally determining to welcome home their providence-chosen brand evangelist. A Truly Natural Fit Keran Checker, the Managing Director of Checkers Africa Limited, the parent company of Checkers Custard, at the signing ceremony in his speech said, “ T emi Nkem is one of a kind; she came, she saw, and conquered the world with her charm and exceptional attitude at Big Brother Naija, and this made us take a deep look into the beautiful and interesting young lady and explore the potential of her representing the brand due to shared values and unparalleled natural alignment ”. item.title: Ghana’s Black Challenge Conquer the World With First-Ever Amputee Football World Cup Title
item.description: Pure joy on the pitch as Ghana’s Black Challenge mark their historic 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup triumph in Mexico. Ghana’s national amputee football team, the Black Challenge, have officially conquered the world after edging Morocco 1–0 in the final of the 2026 World Amputee Football Federation (WAFF) World Cup in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico on Sunday, November 22, 2026. For anyone keeping an eye on international football and West African sporting milestones, this is a moment worth celebrating—it marks Ghana’s very first Amputee Football World Cup crown. The championship match brought together two African powerhouses and served as a high-stakes showdown between familiar rivals, following Ghana’s earlier continental triumphs against Morocco, including the 2024 African Amputee Cup of Nations final. Captain Richard Arthur Opentil stepped up as the decisive hero, scoring the lone goal in the 32nd minute. From there, Ghana dug deep with grit, smart positioning, and defensive discipline to shut out Morocco and bring the trophy home. Intense action between Morocco and Ghana during the 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico. What makes Ghana’s run in Mexico even more memorable is how much they had to overcome in the knockout stages. The Black Challenge defeated the United States 3–1 in the Round of 16, eased past Egypt 2–0 in the quarter-finals behind a brace from forward Mubarik Mohammed , and then edged a tense semi-final 1–1 after extra time before winning 4–3 on penalties. Individual brilliance shone right alongside the team trophy. Forward Mubarik Mohammed finished as the tournament’s top scorer with seven goals, earning the Golden Boot award. Back home, the achievement sparked widespread celebration, with congratulatory messages from Ghana’s leadership—including President John Dramani Mahama and the Ministry of Sports and Recreation—alongside financial backing and pledges from corporate supporters and philanthropists such as Gold Fields Ghana and Mohammed Raii through the EEZZY Group Foundation. Speaking after the victory, captain Richard Arthur Opentil dedicated the triumph to Ghana and its supporters as an early Christmas gift to the nation. Ghana’s Black Challenge celebrate lifting their maiden 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup trophy in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico. If you are wondering what the WAFF Amputee Football World Cup is all about, it is the premier international championship for amputee football, governed globally by the World Amputee Football Federation (WAFF). Played according to rules adapted from FIFA’s Laws of the Game, amputee football is fast-paced, physically demanding, and thrilling to watch. Matches feature seven players per side—outfield players with lower-limb amputations playing on forearm crutches without prostheses, and goalkeepers with single-arm amputations—with crutches treated as part of the player’s body rather than a tool to intentionally play the ball. item.title: Solape Fayemi Launches Saina Properties Across Four Markets
item.description: For many people, buying property is one of the biggest financial decisions they will ever make. Yet, knowing who to trust, how to verify ownership and whether a property is worth the investment can make the process overwhelming. It is a challenge Solape Fayemi hopes to address with the launch of Saina Properties , a real estate company now operating across Nigeria, the United Kingdom, the United States and the United Arab Emirates. Officially unveiled at an event held on 17 November at the Marriott Hotel, Ikeja GRA, Lagos, Saina Properties is built around a simple idea: property ownership should be guided by sound advice, proper verification and professional support, not just the excitement of closing a deal. For Solape, whose experience in the investment industry shaped her understanding of money, risk and wealth creation, the decision to establish the company came from recognising the need for a more considered approach to real estate. “We are not building Saina Properties because the world needs another company selling properties. We are building Saina because we believe there is room for a different kind of real estate experience. One where advice comes before the transaction, where due diligence is not treated as an inconvenience, and where people are encouraged to ask questions, understand their options and make informed decisions,” she said at the launch. That philosophy is reflected in the company’s three core areas of expertise: Advisory & Verification, Sales & Brokerage, and Developments . Rather than focusing solely on connecting buyers to properties, Saina brings together the guidance investors need to assess opportunities, the support required to navigate property transactions, and involvement in real estate development. The company is also building on experience gained before its official launch, having supported more than 25 clients with property opportunities across different markets. An important part of its proposition is the role of professional expertise in protecting property investors. Fayemi’s position raises a familiar question: people consult doctors for medical concerns and lawyers for legal matters, so why do some investors leave significant property decisions in the hands of relatives simply because they are available or familiar with the location? While trust and family relationships matter, they do not automatically translate into the technical knowledge needed to assess a property, verify its documentation or understand its investment potential. These decisions require proper checks, market understanding and accountability. With its operations spanning four markets, Saina Properties aims to support individuals and investors looking to navigate property ownership with greater clarity, whether they are buying, selling or exploring development opportunities. Its guiding promise captures the thinking behind the business: “ With Saina Properties, you own with certainty.” Solape Fayemi is the Chief Executive Officer of Sa

item.title: How Mary Akinwola Graduated with a Distinction from Oxford After Receiving Multiple Scholarships
item.description: Mary Akinwola graduated from the University of Oxford after receiving the Chevening and Mastercard Foundation Scholarships. My name is Mary Akinwola. I’m a physiotherapist, a strategy consultant, a healthcare entrepreneur, and I recently graduated from the University of Oxford with a distinction in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation. I have probably said that last part a hundred times since getting my results, and honestly, I don’t think I’m tired of saying it yet. Haha! One thing about me is that I like to be involved. I am sometimes curious about things that have absolutely nothing to do with what I’m supposed to be doing, and I genuinely enjoy working with people. I like organising things, bringing people together, and seeing an idea move forward to get accomplished. So I have known that going to Oxford was never going to be just about getting a master’s degree. Let me explain how I ended up there. I studied Physiotherapy at the University of Ibadan, where I graduated with First-Class Honours. During my undergraduate years, I was involved in quite a lot outside academics: student leadership, journalism, research, community health programmes and advocacy. My involvement in community health exposed me to how differently people experience healthcare depending on where they live, what they can afford and what information they have access to. I loved being a physiotherapist, and that allowed me to interrogate questions that went beyond individual patient care. Why do some people receive good healthcare while others struggle to access even basic services? How do we make healthcare more affordable? What role can technology play? And why do some seemingly good healthcare programmes struggle to produce lasting change? Eventually, I realised I wanted to study and work in a field that constantly seeks to improve health systems. I researched different programmes across the US and UK, hoping to study at institutions that have international audiences where I could build a diverse perspective in health. I came across the MSc in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation at the University of Oxford’s Nuffield Department of Medicine. It aligned with many of my interests, so I applied. I also needed a scholarship because, quite frankly, I couldn’t afford Oxford. It was a humbling and affirming process. I was awarded scholarships such as the Chevening Scholarship and two Oxford-based scholarships. I still feel fortunate to have received and chosen the Mastercard Foundation-Africa Oxford Initiative Scholarship, which fully funded my studies. I am deeply grateful for that opportunity. Now, I think it’s important to say that I was very excited about the academic programme. I wanted to understand healthcare systems better, learn new research methods and become more effective at designing and evaluating healthcare services. However, I was also very excited about everything else. I was going to be at Oxford! There were going to be people from different countries

item.title: “Money in a Wheelbarrow”: Adekunle Gold & Blaqbonez Are Making Big-Money Talk Sound Good
item.description: Artwork for Adekunle Gold and Blaqbonez’s collaboration “Money in a Wheelbarrow”. Did you ever envisage an Adekunle Gold and Blaqbonez collaboration? You’re not alone, neither did we, but as it turns out, “ Money in a Wheelbarrow ” is officially here—and Adekunle Gold shared that this is actually a link-up with an artist who released a diss track about him years ago, plus their second attempt at making a song together. If you enjoy a track with a cheeky backstory behind it, this one is all about celebrating your hard-earned bag, enjoying the fruits of your grind and soaking up good moments right now instead of putting joy off until later. On the song itself, Adekunle Gold brings his smooth, melodic touch alongside Blaqbonez’s witty rap delivery as they trade lines about stacking cash, containers landing in Apapa and living large. You get a lively mix of English, Nigerian Pidgin and Yoruba phrasing that makes you want to sing along fast, turning big-money talk into something bright and upbeat rather than heavy. The visuals match that playful mood right from the start, with bold pixel-style lettering flashing across the screen over a bright backdrop where both artists are dressed in sharp dark suits, ties, sunglasses and stacks of cash. Watching them pose around wheelbarrows piled with money as words like “Wheel Barrow”, “Pack Am O”, “Container”, “Apapa”, “Hosana” and “Duffel Bag” pop up gives the video a fun, tongue-in-cheek edge that keeps your eyes locked on the screen. I f you want a fresh, upbeat tune with a funny plot twist behind it, “Money in a Wheelbarrow” is ready for your playlist. *** Photo Credit: Adekunle Gold/Instagram The post “Money in a Wheelbarrow”: Adekunle Gold & Blaqbonez Are Making Big-Money Talk Sound Good appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: The Wedding Countdown Is On! Diana Eneje & Pascal Godwin Celebrate Their Introduction in Royal Blue
item.description: Pascal Godwin in Rogue and Diana Eneje in Dova Bridals at their introduction ceremony, styled by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon. Diana Eneje and Pascal Godwin ‘s forever journey has begun, but first of all, introductions! Three months after Pascal proposed against the backdrop of Cape Town’s mountains and vineyards in August 2026, the Nigerian fashion influencer and entrepreneur and her Lagos-based businessman fiancé have taken another lovely step towards walking down the aisle. While they are not married just yet, the couple have officially held their introduction ceremony, bringing both families together ahead of their traditional and white weddings. For anyone unfamiliar with the tradition, the introduction is an important first step in many Nigerian weddings. It is when the couple’s families meet formally, exchange greetings, offer prayers and give their blessings as the relationship moves towards marriage. And while the main wedding celebrations are still ahead, Diana and Pascal have given us a first look at what we can expect from their wedding style. Diana Eneje and Pascal Godwin in coordinated royal blue looks by Dova Bridals and Rogue for their introduction ceremony. If you’ve followed Diana from her early modelling days and her appearance in Rema ‘s 2019 “ Dumebi ” music video to building her beauty brand, The Shine Cartel, you’ll know that fashion is always part of her story. Styled together by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon , the two stepped out in coordinated royal blue looks, with Dova Bridals creating Diana’s introduction dress that brought together lace, colourful woven fabric and satin. Diana Eneje wearing a custom royal blue beaded lace, woven fabric, and satin mermaid gown by Dova Bridals. Her dress featured an off-the-shoulder beaded lace bodice with a sweetheart neckline and short tiered sleeves. From the waist, it flowed into a chevron-patterned woven skirt featuring shades of red, green, gold and blue, before opening into a pleated royal blue satin mermaid hem. She completed the look with a matching beaded fan handbag, silver jewellery with dark stone accents and crystal-strapped blue heels, alongside a sleek updo with sculpted waves. Diana Eneje in her custom Dova Bridals royal blue beaded lace and woven introduction dress, styled by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon and photographed by Chuchu Ojekwe Pascal coordinated with Diana in a custom royal blue velvet traditional robe and trouser set by Rogue . Gold and silver geometric and botanical beadwork ran across the chest, shoulders and sleeves, continuing down to the fringed hem . He finished with a matching beaded cap, layered deep blue beads and a gold pendant, dark-tinted sunglasses, a gold wristwatch and dark velvet loafers, with a tall carved black walking staff completing his traditional look . item.title: Elizabeth Agboola: Your Next Flight From Nigeria Could Be Two Holidays in One. Here’s How
item.description: Have you ever spent six hours in an airport waiting for your connecting flight, watching the departure screens, browsing duty-free shops and wondering what the city outside looks like? Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport. What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. Many Nigerians book international tickets based on price, travel time and baggage allowance. These are important considerations, but there is another question worth asking: What else can this ticket give me? I am talking about stopovers, not the hurried two-hour connection where you are running between terminals, but an intentional break in your journey that allows you to experience another destination before continuing to the country you originally planned to visit. And with the right airline, itinerary and travel documents, that additional experience might cost less than you imagine. First, Understand What You Are Booking A layover is generally a connection between flights; a stopover is a longer, planned break in your journey. Airlines define these differently, and the distinction matters because some offer special hotel packages, sightseeing tours or complimentary accommodation to qualifying passengers. For example, imagine travelling from Lagos to London through Istanbul. Instead of spending a few hours at Istanbul Airport, you could investigate whether your ticket qualifies for a longer stopover, allowing you to explore Istanbul before continuing to London. You have now turned one international journey into an opportunity to experience two destinations outside Nigeria. The secret is to investigate the stopover before purchasing your ticket, rather than arriving at the airport and hoping the airline will allow you to stay longer. Turkish Airlines: Turn Istanbul Into Part of Your Holiday Turkish Airlines operates a Stopover in Istanbul programme for eligible international passengers connecting through Istanbul Airport. For visa purposes, Nigerians do not qualify, but with a valid Turkish visa you would be able to qualify for some of the perks. Qualifying travellers with connections of at least 20 hours and up to seven days may receive complimentary hotel accommodation. Under the standard programme, eligible Economy Class passengers can receive one night in a four-star hotel, while Business Class passengers may receive two nights in a five-star or boutique hotel. Imagine travelling from Abuja or Lagos through Istanbul to London, Paris or another European destination. Rather than treating Istanbul as somewhere you simply change planes, you could plan time to experience the

How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds
item.description: Maurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. item.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
item.description: Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out. It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros. Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz) Processor: Apple M6 RAM: 16, 24 or 32GB Storage: 1, 2 or 4TB SSD Operating system: macOS 26.4 Tahoe Camera: 12MP Centre Stage Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones Dimensions: 221.2 x 312.6 x 15.5mm Weight: 1.55kg Continue reading...

item.title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen
item.description: Redesigned flagship laptop has a fantastic display, killer performance and the first touchscreen on a Mac, but comes with a serious price tag Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac. The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon . item.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
item.description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. Continue reading...

item.title: Superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud
item.description: N44 is a complex nebula filled with glowing hydrogen gas, dark lanes of dust, massive stars, and many populations of stars of different ages. One of its most distinctive features, however, is the dark, starry gap called a “superbubble,” visible in this Hubble Space Telescope image in the upper central region.

item.title: Lunar Occultation of Venus
item.description: On Wednesday, June 17, skywatchers across the United States—and parts of Canada—enjoyed a rare event: a daytime lunar occultation of Venus. A lunar occultation occurs when the Moon moves directly in front of another celestial object from our viewpoint on Earth, briefly hiding it from sight.

item.title: Igniting Roman's Journey
item.description: Now on a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will soon reveal the universe’s darkest secrets. The mission launched at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Aug. 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

item.title: August Lunar Eclipse Rises Over Louisiana
item.description: A lunar eclipse is visible over southern Louisiana. The lunar eclipse was visible throughout much of North and South America and part of Europe and Africa between Aug. 27-28. The Full Moon slipped through Earth’s shadow on Aug. 27, continuing into Aug. 28 for some parts of the world, resulting in the lunar eclipse. At maximum eclipse, the Moon takes on a dramatic dark, ruddy or coppery tint along the covered edge. New Orleans is home to NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility, where stages for NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and structures for Orion spacecraft are produced for the Artemis missions.

item.title: Artemis III RS-25 Engine Processing: #3 Lift
item.description: Technicians prepare to transfer the #2 RS-25 SLS (Space Launch System) rocket engine (front) to the work stand with the #3 engine (back) for integration with the Artemis III core stage rocket on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. During Artemis III, the four RS‑25 engines will launch the Orion spacecraft and its crew of four into low Earth orbit, generating more than two million pounds of thrust at liftoff.
